metadata.title: Building multicultural teaching self-efficacy: Key factors of secondary teachers’ confidence in diverse classrooms

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD TALIS 2018 U.S. data (lower-secondary teachers in grades 7–9) with a nationally representative sample of 2,561 teachers from 165 schools. The manuscript does not report whether TALIS sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the LASSO logistic regression or in the descriptive/ANOVA analyses, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is based on a binary outcome derived from TALIS composite MTSE scores and uses Stata’s lasso logit, the paper does not document a complex-survey weighting strategy; therefore, weighting status remains unclear. The analytic sample is described as including all U.S. TALIS 2018 participating teachers, with continuous predictors standardized prior to LASSO; no additional grade/school-type filtering is reported.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a dichotomized teacher multicultural teaching self-efficacy (MTSE) score created from TALIS survey items, not a cognitive achievement score with plausible values. TALIS self-efficacy is an attitudinal/psychometric scale rather than an ILSA PV-based achievement domain, so PV handling is not applicable by design. The manuscript also does not report any missing-data handling procedure for the MTSE items or predictors (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because survey datasets typically contain item nonresponse.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the U.S. TALIS 2018 dataset and included all 2,561 participating teachers from 165 schools (lower-secondary teachers corresponding to grades 7–9 in the U.S.). The outcome MTSE was constructed from five MTSE items and then dichotomized into higher vs lower MTSE using the composite MTSE score provided by TALIS; continuous predictors were standardized before LASSO. No additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing-item thresholds, teacher-level exclusions) are explicitly described in the provided text.

main_findings.target_variable: Higher vs lower multicultural teaching self-efficacy (binary MTSE)
main_findings.performance_metrics: LASSO logistic regression (CV-LASSO vs minBIC-LASSO vs Adaptive LASSO): test deviance 1.2905 (CV-LASSO) and 1.2905 (minBIC-LASSO) vs 1.2955 (Adaptive LASSO); deviance ratio 0.0681 (CV-LASSO and minBIC-LASSO) vs 0.0645 (Adaptive LASSO). Post-selection significance testing retained EAL/bilingual ITE training; external-observer feedback excluded as not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (U.S.) lower-secondary teacher the study leveraged preparedness for multicultural/multilingual teaching, PD in multicultural/multilingual teaching, school diversity practices, teachers’ minoritized race/ethnicity, and female gender to predict higher vs lower multicultural teaching self-efficacy, finding that these factors were consistently selected by LASSO and that CV-LASSO/minBIC-LASSO achieved slightly better out-of-sample deviance than Adaptive LASSO. This indicates that strengthening language-informed initial preparation and pedagogically grounded professional development, alongside school-level diversity practices, may be key levers for improving teachers’ confidence in multicultural and multilingual classrooms, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 U.S. data for lower-secondary teachers (grades 7–9), using a binary outcome derived from a five-item multicultural teaching self-efficacy (MTSE) scale. Teachers were dichotomized into higher vs lower MTSE, and the authors applied LASSO logistic regression with three tuning/selection strategies (CV-LASSO, minBIC-LASSO, Adaptive LASSO) implemented in Stata. Across models, six variables were retained as strongly associated with higher MTSE: perceived preparedness for multicultural/multilingual teaching, PD in multicultural/multilingual teaching, school diversity practices, minoritized race/ethnicity, female gender, and ITE training in EAL/bilingual education (external-observer feedback was not retained). Predictive performance favored CV-LASSO and minBIC-LASSO, with test deviance of 1.2905 and deviance ratio of 0.0681 versus Adaptive LASSO (test deviance 1.2955; deviance ratio 0.0645). Limitations include lack of reported missing-data handling, no explicit survey-weight documentation, and no explicit multilevel adjustment despite teachers being nested in schools.
